cardiorespiratory capacity (VO2max), a measure of physical fitness, is associated with insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity, and the disposition-index (the product of insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity) across the entire range of glucose tolerance, from normal to diabetes.
low fitness is associated with low insulin sensitivity, high early-phase GSIS, low late-phase GSIS, and low DIOGTT across the entire glucose-tolerance continuum.
cardiorespiratory (CR) fitness is inversely associated with glycemic indices, including fasting glucose, 2-hour glucose, and HbA1C.

understanding the relationship between physical activity, cardiorespiratory function, and the determinants of glycemia.
the relationship between cardiorespiratory (CR) fitness (VO2MAX) and the determinants of glycemia in subjects with a wide range of glucose tolerance.
the relationship between physical fitness and the determinants of glycemia across the glucose tolerance spectrum.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the association between poor cardio-respiratory fitness and impaired pancreatic β-cell compensation in the face of poor glycemic control is present across the entire glucose-tolerance spectrum.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a low VO2 max is associated with low insulin sensitivity, high fasting glucose, and high insulin secretion, which is consistent with previous work.

low cardiorespiratory function is associated with a number of the underlying determinants (insulin resistance, insulin secretion, compensatory insulin secretion, and insulin secretion relative to resistance) of glycemic control.
the relationship between cardiorespiratory capacity and the determinants of glycemia is not linear across the glucose tolerance spectrum.
